claim: Trypanosoma cruzi is the agent of Chagas disease.
source: Trypanosoma cruzi is a kinetoplastid protozoan and the etiologic agent of Chagas disease, one of the neglected and highest impact parasitic infections in the Americas (Pérez-Molina and Molina, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pérez-Molina and Molina, 2018

claim: Chagas disease is one of the neglected and highest impact parasitic infections in the Americas.
source: Trypanosoma cruzi is a kinetoplastid protozoan and the etiologic agent of Chagas disease, one of the neglected and highest impact parasitic infections in the Americas (Pérez-Molina and Molina, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pérez-Molina and Molina, 2018

claim: Chagas disease causes great loss in both health-care costs and disability-adjusted life years.
source: Chagas disease is estimated to cause great loss in both health-care costs and disability-adjusted life years (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2013

claim: Human migration and specific modes of transmission have led to Chagas disease spreading beyond its natural geographical boundaries.
source: Human migration and specific modes of transmission than the canonical vector-based have led to a spreading beyond its natural geographical boundaries, becoming a global issue (Pérez-Molina and Molina, 2018; Bern, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pérez-Molina and Molina, 2018; Bern, 2015

claim: T. cruzi transmission is a zoonosis maintained by numerous species of triatomine insects and different species of mammals.
source: T. cruzi transmission is a zoonosis maintained by numerous species of triatomine insects and different species of mammals (Jansen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jansen et al., 2018

claim: Transmission to humans occurs most frequently by contamination with infected feces from triatomine vectors.
source: This parasite has a complex life cycle, where transmission to humans occurs most frequently by contamination with infected feces from triatomine vectors.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about T. cruzi transmission

claim: Other routes of human infection include congenital, oral, and contaminated transplant tissues and blood products.
source: Other routes of human infection include congenital, oral (mainly consumption of raw contaminated foods), and contaminated transplant tissues and blood products.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about T. cruzi transmission routes

claim: T. cruzi displays a vast, complex repertoire of surface proteins involved in cell invasion and pathogenicity.
source: To evade the immune responses, the parasite displays a vast, complex repertoire of surface proteins involved in cell invasion and pathogenicity (De Pablos and Osuna, 2012; Pech-Canul et al., 2017; Talavera-López et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Pablos and Osuna, 2012; Pech-Canul et al., 2017; Talavera-López et al., 2021

claim: The regions of the T. cruzi genome coding for surface molecules are composed of highly repetitive sequences.
source: The regions of the genome coding for these molecules are composed of highly repetitive sequences, with hundreds to thousands of members of each family, as well as substantial numbers of transposable elements, microsatellite, and tandem repeats (Talavera-López et al., 2021; El-Sayed et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Talavera-López et al., 2021; El-Sayed et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2021

claim: Both preponderate clonal evolution and sexual reproduction have been proposed for T. cruzi.
source: The reproductive mode of these parasitic protozoans has been widely debated, and both preponderate clonal evolution (Tibayrenc and Ayala, 2012; Tibayrenc and Ayala, 2013) and sexual reproduction (Ramírez and Llewellyn, 2014; Schwabl et al., 2019; Inbar et al., 2019) have been proposed.
evidence: Supported by citations to Tibayrenc and Ayala, 2012; Tibayrenc and Ayala, 2013 for clonal evolution and Ramírez and Llewellyn, 2014; Schwabl et al., 2019; Inbar et al., 2019 for sexual reproduction

claim: Many eukaryotic pathogens have essentially clonal population structures while also having non-obligate sexual cycles.
source: Many eukaryotic pathogens have essentially clonal population structures while also having non-obligate sexual cycles, which may enable them to adapt to environmental changes (Heitman, 2006; Lewis et al., 2011; Steensels et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heitman, 2006; Lewis et al., 2011; Steensels et al., 2021

claim: The most well-studied mating system in trypanosomatids is that of Trypanosoma brucei.
source: In trypanosomatids, the most well-studied mating system is that of Trypanosoma brucei, for which a meiotic process is well supported based on the identification of a haploid parasite stage in the vector (Peacock et al., 2014) and on the patterns of allele inheritance and recombination observed in experimental hybrids (MacLeod et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Peacock et al., 2014 and MacLeod et al., 2005

claim: Six distinct genetic clades of T. cruzi have been recognized, named TcI to TcVI.
source: In T. cruzi, great genetic and phenotypic diversity is observed, and six distinct genetic clades have been recognized, named TcI to TcVI (discrete typing units or DTU-I to -VI) (Zingales et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zingales et al., 2012

claim: TcV and TcVI are recent, natural inter-lineage hybrids of TcII and TcIII.
source: Genotyping analysis indicates that TcV and TcVI are recent, natural inter-lineage hybrids of TcII and TcIII, showing that recombination events have shaped the evolution of T. cruzi lineages (Schwabl et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 2011; Messenger and Miles, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwabl et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 2011; Messenger and Miles, 2015

claim: The formation of T. cruzi hybrids in vitro has been described.
source: In addition to natural evidence of hybridization, the formation of T. cruzi hybrids in vitro was also described (Gaunt et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gaunt et al., 2003

claim: Genetic marker analyses of hybrid strains showed multi-allelic (non-Mendelian) inheritance of microsatellite alleles and an elevated DNA content.
source: Genetic marker analyses of hybrid strains showed multi-allelic (non-Mendelian) inheritance of microsatellite alleles and an elevated DNA content (Gaunt et al., 2003; Lewis et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gaunt et al., 2003; Lewis et al., 2009

claim: The hybridization events in T. cruzi were proposed to occur via a parasexual mechanism, similar to those observed in certain fungi.
source: The hybridization events in T. cruzi were proposed to occur via a parasexual mechanism, similar to those observed in certain fungi (Lewis et al., 2011; Steensels et al., 2021; Gaunt et al., 2003; Bennett, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2011; Steensels et al., 2021; Gaunt et al., 2003; Bennett, 2015

claim: Two closely related TcI strains (P1, P2) and three hybrid clones (1C2, 1D12, 2C1) were selected for the study.
source: To investigate the effects of clonal reproduction and genetic exchange on the T. cruzi genome at the microevolutionary scale, we selected two closely related TcI strains (P1, P2) and three hybrid clones that were generated from a P1 × P2 cross (1C2, 1D12, 2C1) (Gaunt et al., 2003).
evidence: Describes the experimental design and materials used in the study

claim: The two parents and three hybrids were continuously cultured as epimastigote forms for 5 years, equivalent to approximately 800 generations.
source: The two parents and three hybrids were included in an in vitro evolution experiment in which they were continuously cultured as epimastigote forms for 5 years, equivalent to approximately 800 generations of replication by binary fission (Figure 1A).
evidence: Describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A

claim: The DNA content of the two parental lines remained approximately constant during the microevolution experiment.
source: We observed that the DNA content of the two parental lines remained approximately constant (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B-D

claim: At the start of the experiment, the total DNA content of the hybrid clones was approximately 70% greater than the parentals.
source: At the start of the experiment, the total DNA content of the hybrid clones was approximately 70% greater than the parentals (Figure 1C, D, Lewis et al., 2009), which equated to slightly below expectations for a tetraploid parasite with one kinetoplast (containing mitochondrial DNA), that is, a 4n1k (4C) genome size.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C, D and citation to Lewis et al., 2009

claim: The DNA content of the hybrids became progressively lower over time, up to a maximum decrease of 22.5% by generation 800.
source: Over the course of the microevolution experiment, in contrast to P1 and P2, we found that the DNA content of the hybrids became progressively lower over time, up to a maximum decrease of 22.5% by generation 800.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry measurements over time

claim: Genome erosion in the hybrids occurred at an average rate of 23 kb per generation.
source: By extrapolation from the estimated genome sizes of P1 (94.5 Mb) and P2 (92.5 Mb) (Lewis et al., 2009), these data indicate genome erosion in the hybrids occurred at an average rate of 23 kb per generation.
evidence: Calculated from flow cytometry data and genome size estimates from Lewis et al., 2009

claim: Hybrid 2C1 showed gradual genome erosion at each time point, with all three 800 generation evolved clones approximating a 3C genome size.
source: Hybrid 2C1 showed gradual genome erosion at each time point, with all three 800 generation evolved clones approximating a 3C genome size.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data over time

claim: Hybrid 1C2 showed a more intermittent pattern of genome erosion, with most erosion occurring between 0–200 and 400–600 generations.
source: Hybrid 1C2 showed a more intermittent pattern – most of the erosion occurred between 0–200 and 400–600 generations, reaching a 3C genome size, but interestingly, 2 of the 800 generation clones gained ~10% more DNA than at t=600.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data over time

claim: Hybrid 1D12 had an initial 9% loss between t=0 and t=200, but was then quite stable over time between 3C and 4C.
source: Lastly, hybrid 1D12 had an initial 9% loss between t=0 and t=200, but was then quite stable over time between 3C and 4C.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data over time

claim: Three of the nine evolved hybrid clones had lost at least one microsatellite allele.
source: We found that three of the nine evolved hybrid clones had lost at least one microsatellite allele (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by microsatellite genotyping data in Supplementary file 1

claim: The haploid estimated genome size of P1 differed from P2 by approximately 2 Mbp.
source: The haploid estimated genome size of P1 differed from P2 by approximately 2 Mbp, and both parental strains genomes were found to be slightly larger than the 44 Mbp reference TcI-Sylvio X10/1 strain (Talavera-López et al., 2021), in line with flow cytometry-based DNA content measurements (Lewis et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by genome assembly data and citations to Talavera-López et al., 2021 and Lewis et al., 2009

claim: The genome-wide average SNP density was 9.28 and 3.71 SNP/kb for P1 and P2, respectively.
source: The resultant genome-wide average SNP density was 9.28 and 3.71 SNP/kb for P1 and P2, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by SNP calling data shown in Table 1

claim: Most SNPs were located within repetitive regions, particularly in areas containing surface molecule gene family members.
source: Most SNPs were located within repetitive regions, particularly in areas containing surface molecule gene family members, which can be related to gene expansion in these regions.
evidence: Inferred from SNP distribution analysis

claim: P1 displays tandem-repeated and surface molecule-coding regions expanded in comparison to P2.
source: Indeed, copy number variation (CNV) analysis showed that P1 displays these tandem-repeated and surface molecule-coding regions expanded in comparison to P2.
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis data

claim: SNP density in high-quality mapping regions was 2.84 and 2.11 SNPs/kb for P1 and P2, respectively.
source: SNP density in the retained high-quality regions was 2.84 and 2.11 SNPs/kb for P1 and P2, respectively (Table 1), and a total of 68,616 and 34,843 SNPs exclusive for each parental strain were catalogued for use in the analysis of the hybrid strains (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by SNP calling data shown in Table 1 and Figure 1E

claim: The average SNP density in high-quality mapping regions was higher in all hybrids than in parental strains.
source: The average SNP density in these regions was higher in all hybrids than in parental strains: 3.48 SNP/kb for 1C2-0, 3.29 SNP/kb for 1D12-0, and 3.49 SNP/kb for 2C1-0 (Table 1), partially due to the presence of alleles from both parental strains.
evidence: Supported by SNP calling data shown in Table 1

claim: Additional SNPs common to all hybrids and SNPs exclusive to each hybrid clone were identified in both coding and non-coding regions.
source: In addition to the SNPs clearly inherited from each parental strain, additional SNPs common to all hybrids and SNPs exclusive to each hybrid clone were identified in both coding and non-coding regions, revealing sample-specific patterns (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by SNP analysis data shown in Figure 1E

claim: De novo mutations common to all hybrids and exclusive to each hybrid clone were predicted to generate a higher percentage of non-synonymous changes compared to mutations inherited from the parental strains.
source: Interestingly, de novo mutations common to all hybrids and exclusive to each hybrid clone were predicted to generate a higher percentage of non-synonymous changes in comparison to the mutations inherited from the parental strains (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by SNP effect prediction data in Supplementary file 3

claim: The ratio of non-synonymous changes per synonymous changes was higher in de novo mutations than in those inherited from the parental strains.
source: Indeed, the ratio of non-synonymous changes per synonymous changes was higher in the de novo mutations common to all hybrids (2.36 for 1C2-0, 2.25 for 1D12-0, and 2.19 for 2C1-0), and exclusive to each hybrid clone (2.40 for 1C2-0, 2.23 for 1D12-0, and 2.37 for 2C1-0) than in those inherited from the parental strains (1.41 for 1C2-0, 1.40 for 1D12-0, and 1.42 for 2C1-0) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by SNP effect prediction data in Supplementary file 3

claim: The ratio of surface protein-coding genes per non-surface protein-coding genes is approximately 4-fold higher in SNPs common to all hybrids and in SNPs exclusive to each hybrid clone than in those inherited from the parental strains.
source: This ratio is approximately 4-fold higher in SNPs common to all hybrids and in SNPs exclusive to each hybrid clone than in those inherited from the parental strains (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by SNP distribution analysis in Supplementary file 4

claim: The ratio of non-synonymous mutations in surface protein-coding genes per non-synonymous mutations in other genes was approximately 3.3-fold higher in the hybrid clone-specific SNPs compared to those inherited from the parental strains.
source: Interestingly, this ratio was approximately 3.3-fold higher in the hybrid clone-specific SNPs in comparison to those inherited from the parental strains (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by SNP distribution analysis in Supplementary file 5

claim: Aneuploidy was observed in the P2 strain, involving trisomy of chromosomes 2 and 21.
source: Aneuploidy was observed in the P2 strain, involving trisomy of chromosomes 2 and 21 (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by RDC and AB analysis shown in Figure 2A, B

claim: The RDC analysis indicated aneuploidy in chromosome 44 in the P1 strain.
source: The RDC analysis indicated aneuploidy in chromosome 44 in the P1 strain, but due to the lack of regions with high-quality SNPs, it was not possible to confirm this in the AB analysis (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by RDC analysis shown in Figure 2A, B, but not confirmed by AB analysis

claim: In both parental strains, a peak at 50% was observed in allele balance analysis, while in the hybrids, peaks at 25% and 75% or 50% were observed.
source: In both parental strains, a peak at 50% was observed, while in the hybrids, peaks at 25% and 75% or 50% were observed (Figure 2C), which is expected for diploid and tetraploid genomes, respectively (Reis-Cunha and Bartholomeu, 2019).
evidence: Supported by allele balance analysis shown in Figure 2C and citation to Reis-Cunha and Bartholomeu, 2019

claim: The hybrids displayed ~70% greater DNA content than the parental strains based on flow cytometry.
source: This ploidy estimation is in accordance with the previous DNA content estimation based on flow cytometry data, in which the hybrids displayed ~70% greater DNA content than the parental strains (Figure 1C, Lewis et al., 2009), given that this method could not determine the relative amounts of mitochondrial kDNA and nuclear DNA.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and citation to Lewis et al., 2009

claim: Inheritance of SNPs exclusive to both parental strains were observed in the hybrid genomes.
source: Inheritance of SNPs exclusive to both parental strains were observed in the hybrid genomes (Figure 1E), which shows that the tetrasomic profile observed resulted from a contribution from both parental chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by SNP inheritance analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: The trisomies in chromosomes 2 and 21 of P2 were no longer observed in any replicate clone after growth in culture.
source: The trisomies in chromosomes 2 and 21 of P2 (Figure 2A) were no longer observed in any replicate clone after growth in culture (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by CCNV analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4A

claim: New aneuploidies were identified in the parental strains after culture growth, involving trisomy of chromosomes 37 and 45 in all P1 clones and trisomy of chromosomes 32 and 37 in all P2 clones.
source: New aneuploidies were identified in the parental strains, involving trisomy of chromosomes 37 and 45 in all P1 clones and trisomy of chromosomes 32 and 37 in all P2 clones (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by CCNV analysis shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: Hybrid 2C1 displayed a clear transition from a tetraploid to a triploid pattern after growth in culture.
source: Indeed, hybrid 2C1 displayed a clear transition from a tetraploid to a triploid pattern after growth in culture (Figure 4C), suggesting that genome erosion eventually leads to a return towards diploidy after the hybridization event, as observed in the naturally occurring TcV and TcVI hybrids (Lewis et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by ploidy estimation shown in Figure 4C and citation to Lewis et al., 2009

claim: Tetrasomic profiles in chromosomes 19 and 37 were present in all hybrid clones after culture growth.
source: Despite the patterns of genome erosion, tetrasomic profiles in chromosomes 19 and 37 were present in all hybrid clones after culture growth (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by CCNV analysis shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: The genome erosion seems to be gradual phenomena, with sequential losses of chromosome copies and regions rather than coordinated jumps between ploidy levels.
source: Taken together with previous DNA content analysis of intermediate time points (Figure 1), our results from the different in vitro evolved clones indicate that the genome erosion seems to be gradual phenomena, with sequential losses of chromosome copies and regions rather than coordinated jumps between ploidy levels.
evidence: Inferred from flow cytometry and CCNV data over time shown in Figure 1

claim: Similar gene categories showed CNV in both parental and hybrid clones after culture growth.
source: Despite the stability of DNA content in parental clones during our experiment (Figure 1C, D), similar gene categories showed CNV in both parental and hybrid clones after culture growth (Supplementary files 6–12).
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis data in Supplementary files 6-12

claim: Gene losses occurred mainly in host-parasite interaction genes such as surface protein-coding genes and genes related to exocytosis and cell secretion.
source: Gene losses occurred mainly in host-parasite interaction genes such as surface protein-coding genes and genes related to exocytosis and cell secretion, while genes related to macromolecule metabolism, ion transport, and cell division showed an increase in copy numbers (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Genes related to macromolecule metabolism, ion transport, and cell division showed an increase in copy numbers after culture growth.
source: Gene losses occurred mainly in host-parasite interaction genes such as surface protein-coding genes and genes related to exocytosis and cell secretion, while genes related to macromolecule metabolism, ion transport, and cell division showed an increase in copy numbers (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Chromosomes 19 and 37 remained tetrasomic in all hybrid clones after culture growth.
source: Despite the events of genome erosion, chromosomes 19 and 37 remained tetrasomic in all hybrid clones and an extra copy of chromosome 37 is observed in all parental clones after culture growth (Figure 4B and Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by CCNV analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 5B

claim: Chromosomes 19 and 37 contain long core regions with abundant housekeeping genes involved in cellular metabolism, DNA replication and transcription.
source: Chromosomes 19 and 37 contain long core regions with abundant housekeeping genes involved in cellular metabolism, DNA replication and transcription (Supplementary files 10 and 11) which may contribute to fitness in culture.
evidence: Supported by gene content analysis in Supplementary files 10 and 11

claim: All P1 replicates showed a similar SNP density in the retained high-quality regions after culture growth.
source: Regarding the parental strains, all P1 replicates showed a similar SNP density in the retained high-quality regions after culture growth (P1-0: 2.84; P1-1: 2.80; P1-2: 2.77; P1-3: 2.82), while all P2 replicates showed an increase in SNP density after culture growth (P2-0: 2.11; P2-1 2.78; P2-2 2.81; P2-3 2.66, Mann-Whitney, p=0.042) (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by SNP density analysis shown in Figure 7A with statistical test

claim: All P2 replicates showed an increase in SNP density after culture growth.
source: Regarding the parental strains, all P1 replicates showed a similar SNP density in the retained high-quality regions after culture growth (P1-0: 2.84; P1-1: 2.80; P1-2: 2.77; P1-3: 2.82), while all P2 replicates showed an increase in SNP density after culture growth (P2-0: 2.11; P2-1 2.78; P2-2 2.81; P2-3 2.66, Mann-Whitney, p=0.042) (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by SNP density analysis shown in Figure 7A with statistical test

claim: The P2 replicates have a reduction in copies of HUS1-like encoding genes after culture growth.
source: The P2 replicates have a reduction in copies of HUS1-like encoding genes, which are involved in DNA repair, after culture growth (Supplementary file 12).
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis in Supplementary file 12

claim: Many HUS1-like genes were located on chromosome 2.
source: Our gene enrichment analysis showed that a number of these genes were located on chromosome 2 (Supplementary file 12), suggesting that the loss of trisomy in this chromosome could possibly have contributed to the higher number of mutations that was found in the P2 clones.
evidence: Supported by gene enrichment analysis in Supplementary file 12

claim: All evolved hybrid replicate clones, with exception of 1D12-3, showed a slight decrease in SNP density.
source: All evolved hybrid replicate clones, with exception of 1D12-3, showed a slight decrease in SNP density (1C2-0: 3.48; 1C2-1: 2.96; 1C2-2: 3.26; 1C2-3: 3.10; 1D12-0: 3.29; 1D12-1: 3.24; 1D12-2: 3.22; 1D12-3: 3.36; 2C1-0: 3.49; 2C1-1: 3.34; 2C1-2: 2.64; 2C1-3: 3.25, Figure 7A), likely caused by the loss of genetic material.
evidence: Supported by SNP density analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: Multiple new genomic variants were found in the in vitro evolved hybrid progeny, displaying patterns specific to each clonal isolate.
source: Multiple new genomic variants were found in the in vitro evolved hybrid progeny, displaying patterns specific to each clonal isolate (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by SNP analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: The SNP density pattern per chromosome remained similar for all samples in first generation (t=0) and after culture growth (t=800).
source: The SNP density pattern per chromosome remained similar for all samples in first generation (t=0) and after culture growth (t=800).
evidence: Inferred from chromosome-level SNP density analysis

claim: Some chromosomes (e.g. chromosomes 5, 11, 24, and 37) display higher SNP density than the others across all samples.
source: Some chromosomes (e.g. chromosomes 5, 11, 24, and 37) display higher SNP density than the others across all samples (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by chromosome-level SNP density analysis shown in Figure 7B

claim: P2 evolved clone replicates had an increase in SNP density in nearly all chromosomes.
source: P2 evolved clone replicates had an increase in SNP density in nearly all chromosomes (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by chromosome-level SNP density analysis shown in Figure 7B

claim: The emergence of novel SNPs after culture growth resulted in most of the non-synonymous mutations.
source: The emergence of novel SNPs after culture growth resulted in most of the non-synonymous mutations.
evidence: Inferred from SNP effect prediction analysis

claim: The regions of the genome with higher genetic variation in all clone isolates contain surface protein-coding sequences.
source: Interestingly, the regions of the genome with higher genetic variation in all clone isolates contain surface protein-coding sequences (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by SNP distribution analysis shown in Figure 7C

claim: The ratio of non-synonymous mutations in surface protein-coding genes to non-synonymous mutations in other genes was higher for the mutations that appeared in each evolved parental clone compared to those present in the first generation.
source: This ratio was higher for the mutations that appeared in each evolved parental clone in comparison to those present in the first generation (approx. 2.5-fold higher for P1 clones and 3.5-fold higher for P2 clones; Supplementary file 13).
evidence: Supported by SNP distribution analysis in Supplementary file 13

claim: A similar ratio of non-synonymous mutations in surface protein-coding genes to other genes was observed in the SNPs that appeared in each evolved hybrid clone and those exclusive to each hybrid clone present in the first generation.
source: Regarding the hybrid strains, a similar ratio was observed in the SNPs that appeared in each evolved hybrid clone and those exclusive to each hybrid clone present in the first generation (Supplementary file 13).
evidence: Supported by SNP distribution analysis in Supplementary file 13

claim: Surface molecule-coding regions may mutate faster than the rest of the genome either by clonal or parasexual mechanisms.
source: These results indicate that surface molecule-coding regions may mutate faster than the rest of the genome either by clonal or parasexual mechanisms, representing an important region of genomic diversification.
evidence: Inferred from SNP distribution and mutation rate analysis

claim: All initial hybrid clones were essentially tetraploid.
source: The results from whole genome sequencing analysis of this T. cruzi genetic cross have clearly demonstrated that, while the parental strains were diploid, all initial hybrid clones were essentially tetraploid.
evidence: Supported by ploidy estimation from allele balance and flow cytometry data

claim: Genomic variants exclusive to both parental strains were present in all hybrid clones, indicating that the tetraploid profile resulted from the fusion of the two disomic parental genomes.
source: We showed that genomic variants exclusive to both parental strains were present in all hybrid clones, indicating that the tetraploid profile observed is obtained by the fusion of the two disomic parental genomes, although more complex pathways cannot be ruled out in the absence of direct observational evidence.
evidence: Inferred from SNP inheritance patterns

claim: Genome erosion seems to be gradual, with sequential losses of chromosome copies rather than coordinated jumps between ploidy levels.
source: In addition, we showed that genome erosion seems to be gradual, with sequential losses of chromosome copies rather than coordinated jumps between ploidy levels, though with some variation in erosion rates between different evolved hybrid lines.
evidence: Inferred from flow cytometry and CCNV data over time

claim: Hybridization in T. cruzi happened via a parasexual mechanism rather than a canonical meiotic process.
source: As previously proposed (Lewis et al., 2011; Gaunt et al., 2003), our results confirmed that hybridization in T. cruzi happened via a parasexual mechanism rather than a canonical meiotic process.
evidence: Supported by ploidy and inheritance data, with citations to Lewis et al., 2011; Gaunt et al., 2003

claim: The hybridization phenomenon in T. cruzi resembles the parasexual cycle of the pathogenic fungus Candida albicans.
source: This phenomenon resembles the parasexual cycle of the pathogenic fungus Candida albicans, which also involves diploid fusion followed by non-meiotic genome reduction back to aneuploids and diploids (reviewed by Bennett, 2015).
evidence: Comparison to known mechanism in C. albicans, supported by citation to Bennett, 2015

claim: Hybridization in T. brucei and possibly in Leishmania spp. has been associated with parental strains having undergone a meiosis-like process followed by a fusion of haploid cells.
source: In contrast, hybridization in T. brucei and possibly in Leishmania spp. has been associated with parental strains having undergone a meiosis-like process followed by a fusion of haploid cells (Inbar et al., 2019; Peacock et al., 2014; Gibson et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2014; Louradour et al., 2020; Van den Broeck et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Inbar et al., 2019; Peacock et al., 2014; Gibson et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2014; Louradour et al., 2020; Van den Broeck et al., 2020

claim: T. cruzi genomes are highly responsive to the environmental conditions.
source: Our microevolution experiment has shown that T. cruzi genomes are highly responsive to the environmental conditions.
evidence: Inferred from CNV and CCNV changes observed during culture growth

claim: While surface gene numbers were being eroded after culture growth, genes involved in cell metabolism, cell division, and ion transport were being expanded.
source: The CNV analysis showed that while surface gene numbers were being eroded after culture growth, genes involved in cell metabolism, cell division, and ion transport were being expanded.
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis data

claim: Aneuploidies have been widely reported in natural T. cruzi populations.
source: Indeed, aneuploidies have been widely reported in natural T. cruzi populations, and although CCNV varies among and within DTUs, it seems constant within a given population (Schwabl et al., 2019; Reis-Cunha et al., 2015; Reis-Cunha et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwabl et al., 2019; Reis-Cunha et al., 2015; Reis-Cunha et al., 2018

claim: In trypanosomatids, aneuploidy represents an important mechanism for rapidly overcoming environmental diversity.
source: While in many multicellular organisms, aneuploidy is known to have severe consequences, in trypanosomatids it represents an important mechanism for rapidly overcoming environmental diversity (Reis-Cunha et al., 2018; Prieto Barja et al., 2017; Bussotti et al., 2018; Grünebast and Clos, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reis-Cunha et al., 2018; Prieto Barja et al., 2017; Bussotti et al., 2018; Grünebast and Clos, 2020

claim: Aneuploidy is reversed quickly once the benefits of an extra chromosome expire.
source: Aneuploidy is reversed quickly once the benefits of an extra chromosome expire, as observed in P2 aneuploidies in chromosomes 2 and 21.
evidence: Inferred from observation of aneuploidy loss in P2 after culture growth

claim: Trypanosomatids may control overexpression caused by additional gene copies at the protein level.
source: In addition, trypanosomatids may control overexpression caused by additional gene copies, at the protein level (Dumetz, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dumetz, 2017

claim: Aneuploidy in chromosome 37 was found in all parental and hybrid clones after culture growth, suggesting a benefit to parasite fitness in culture.
source: We found aneuploidy in chromosome 37 in all parental and hybrid clones after culture growth, suggesting a benefit to parasite fitness in culture.
evidence: Inferred from consistent observation of chromosome 37 aneuploidy across all clones

claim: In Leishmania spp., the fixation of genetic alterations is the result of positive selection processes that adapt parasite fitness to a given ecology or transmission cycle.
source: As observed in Leishmania spp., the fixation of genetic alterations is the result of positive selection processes that adapt parasite fitness to a given ecology or transmission cycle (Bussotti et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bussotti et al., 2018

claim: An increase in genetic sequence diversity was present after hybridization.
source: Genome variant analyses showed that an increase in genetic sequence diversity was present after hybridization.
evidence: Supported by SNP density analysis

claim: Hybridization events are associated with a burst of novel mutations and a myriad of genomic rearrangements in distinct eukaryotes.
source: Hybridization events are associated with a burst of novel mutations and a myriad of genomic rearrangements (e.g. transpositions, genome size changes, chromosomal rearrangements) in distinct eukaryotes (Steensels et al., 2021; Samarasinghe et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steensels et al., 2021; Samarasinghe et al., 2020

claim: The process of T. cruzi hybrid formation included both new mutations and most likely recombination between parental chromosomes.
source: Our results indicate that the process of T. cruzi hybrid formation included both new mutations and most likely recombination between parental chromosomes.
evidence: Inferred from SNP patterns and inheritance data

claim: There was an increase in the number of SNPs in the hybrid strains with the accumulation of amino acid substitutions.
source: Here, we were able to show an increase in the number of SNPs in the hybrid strains with the accumulation of amino acid substitutions.
evidence: Supported by SNP and effect prediction analysis

claim: The numbers of new SNPs in culture showed a clear difference between the two parental strains after 800 generations, in which P2 showed a higher mutation rate.
source: Interestingly, the numbers of new SNPs in culture showed a clear difference between the two parental strains after 800 generations, in which P2 showed a higher mutation rate.
evidence: Supported by SNP density analysis over time

claim: TcI strains have a mismatch repair machinery that is more efficient than in other DTUs.
source: A previous study has reported that TcI strains have a mismatch repair machinery, which repairs base misincorporation and erroneous insertions and deletions during DNA recombination and replication, that is more efficient than in other DTUs (Reis-Cunha et al., 2015; Augusto-Pinto et al., 2003; Machado et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reis-Cunha et al., 2015; Augusto-Pinto et al., 2003; Machado et al., 2006

claim: In Leishmania major, HUS1 was shown to be required for genome stability under non-stressed conditions and its suppression had a genome-wide mutagenic effect.
source: As described in Leishmania major, HUS1 was shown to be required for genome stability under non-stressed conditions and its suppression had a genome-wide mutagenic effect (Damasceno et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Damasceno et al., 2018

claim: The loss of trisomy in chromosome 2 after culture growth could possibly be related to the increase in mutations observed in the P2 clones.
source: Since many of the genes coding for the HUS1-like proteins are encoded on chromosome 2, the loss of trisomy in this chromosome after culture growth could possibly be related to the increase in mutations observed in the P2 clones.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between HUS1 gene loss and increased mutation rate

claim: Culture growth led to a reduction in genetic variants in nearly all evolved clones in comparison to the first generation.
source: In general, culture growth led to a reduction in genetic variants in nearly all evolved clones in comparison to the first generation.
evidence: Supported by SNP density analysis over time

claim: The reduction in genetic variants may be related to the loss of heterozygosity and the loss of gene copies and genome erosion of surface molecules regions after culture growth.
source: This reduction may be related to the loss of heterozygosity, but also to the loss of gene copies and genome erosion of surface molecules regions after culture growth.
evidence: Inferred from SNP and CNV analysis

claim: There was no bias in the loss of a specific parental chromosome even in triploid hybrid clones, suggesting recombination between the parental chromosomes.
source: In addition, we could not identify any bias in the loss of a specific parental chromosome even in triploid hybrid clones, suggesting recombination between the parental chromosomes.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of parental allele retention patterns

claim: The hybrid clones would likely stabilize at diploidy and contain chromosomes from both parental strains, with a higher polymorphism than the parental strains.
source: As material from both parental strains has been lost during over 800 generations, it is likely that the hybrid clones would stabilize at diploidy and contain chromosomes from both parental strains, with a higher polymorphism than the parental strains.
evidence: Inferred from genome erosion patterns and comparison to natural hybrids

claim: Strains from TcV and TcVI clades have diploid genomes with high repeat content, and high levels of polymorphism in many regions.
source: This is similar to strains from the known natural hybrid clades, TcV and TcVI. Strains from these clades have diploid genomes with high repeat content, and high levels of polymorphism in many regions, resulting from alleles from two divergent parental strains (from clades TcII and TcIII) (Lewis et al., 2011; Messenger and Miles, 2015; Lewis et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2011; Messenger and Miles, 2015; Lewis et al., 2009

claim: The in vitro hybrid formation is highly similar to the process that generated the natural hybrids.
source: From our analyses, it thus appears that the in vitro hybrid formation presented here is highly similar to the process that generated the natural hybrids.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experimental hybrids to natural hybrids

claim: Surface protein-coding genes represent the regions of the genome with higher genetic diversity and more rapid evolution.
source: Our microevolution experiment has shown that surface protein-coding genes represent the regions of the genome with higher genetic diversity and more rapid evolution.
evidence: Supported by SNP distribution and mutation rate analysis

claim: Accumulations of distinct genomic signatures and amino acid substitutions were observed in both parental and hybrid clones after relatively few generations.
source: Accumulations of distinct genomic signatures and amino acid substitutions were observed in both parental and hybrid clones after relatively few generations.
evidence: Supported by SNP analysis over time

claim: There is a higher frequency of recombination in repeat-rich regions of the T. cruzi genome.
source: We have previously observed that there is a higher frequency of recombination in repeat-rich regions of the T. cruzi genome (Talavera-López et al., 2021), and it is likely that this is also the case for the hybrids.
evidence: Supported by citation to Talavera-López et al., 2021 and inference to hybrids

claim: Recent comparative genomics of natural T. cruzi strains have shown a similar pattern of rapid evolution in surface protein-coding regions.
source: Recent comparative genomics of natural T. cruzi strains have shown a similar pattern, suggesting that these regions indeed evolve more rapidly than other regions of the genome (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021

claim: There is clear evidence for relatively recent inter-DTU hybridization between TcII and TcIII as the origin of TcV and TcVI.
source: For T. cruzi, there is clear evidence for relatively recent inter-DTU hybridization between TcII and TcIII as the origin of TcV and TcVI, which are now widespread in domestic transmission cycles in southern South America (Lewis et al., 2011; Messenger and Miles, 2015; Carrasco et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2011; Messenger and Miles, 2015; Carrasco et al., 1996

claim: Evidence for inter-DTU genetic exchange between TcI and TcIV comes from phylogenetic incongruence between nuclear and mitochondrial sequences.
source: Other evidence for inter-DTU genetic exchange between TcI and TcIV comes from phylogenetic incongruence between nuclear and mitochondrial (kDNA maxicircle) sequences.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The frequency of natural genetic exchange events between lineages/clades/DTUs appears to be too low to disrupt the overall stability of the main six clades.
source: However, the frequency of natural genetic exchange events between lineages/clades/DTUs appears to be too low to disrupt the overall stability of the main six clades, or seven clades if the TcBat lineage is included (Lewis et al., 2011; Messenger and Miles, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2011; Messenger and Miles, 2015

claim: The robustness of the clades is likely promoted by ecological and/or geographical isolation.
source: The robustness of the other clades is likely promoted by ecological and/or geographical isolation, for example, association with distinct vector and host species.
evidence: Speculative inference about factors maintaining clade stability

claim: There may be a high fitness cost for tetraploidy in the wild that is not replicated in laboratory conditions.
source: There may also be a high fitness cost for tetraploidy in the wild that is not replicated in laboratory conditions.
evidence: Speculative inference about fitness costs

claim: In vitro hybrid formation in T. cruzi happened in a parasexual mechanism, representing an important mechanism of genetic diversification.
source: In summary, we confirmed that in vitro hybrid formation in T. cruzi happened in a parasexual mechanism, representing an important mechanism of genetic diversification.
evidence: Summary conclusion supported by ploidy and inheritance data

claim: Tetraploid hybrids showed patterns of progressive genome erosion shaped by the environment's selective pressure.
source: Tetraploid hybrids showed patterns of progressive genome erosion shaped by the environment's selective pressure, which may explain distinct phenotypes in isolated natural hybrid populations.
evidence: Summary conclusion supported by flow cytometry and CNV data

claim: An increase in coding sequence diversity is observed in hybrids in comparison to the parental strains, related to both new mutations and most likely recombination events.
source: In addition, an increase in coding sequence diversity is observed in hybrids in comparison to the parental strains, related to both new mutations and most likely recombination events.
evidence: Summary conclusion supported by SNP analysis

claim: Repetitive gene families related to immune evasion evolved more rapidly than other regions of the genome.
source: Finally, our microevolution experiment has shown that repetitive gene families related to immune evasion evolved more rapidly than other regions of the genome, indicating an intrinsic mechanism of genetic variation of these regions.
evidence: Summary conclusion supported by SNP distribution and mutation rate analysis
